paper_title: Koopman Generative Operators for Efficient Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Probabilistic time-series forecasting requires models that simultaneously capture structured temporal dynamics, expressive uncertainty, and efficient inference, yet existing approaches fall short of this goal: latent dynamical models impose structure but rely on restrictive generation mechanisms, while modern generative methods such as diffusion and flow matching achieve flexibility at the cost of iterative and computationally expensive sampling. We introduce the Koopman Generative Operator (KGO), a probabilistic forecasting method that conceptualizes prediction as the evolution of structured uncertainty. KGO integrates three core components: (1) Koopman Patch Embedding (KoPE) for temporally consistent latent trajectory extrapolation; (2) Koopman Flow Matching (KoFM), which enables fast, single-step generation through a closed-form matrix exponential in a Koopman latent space, bypassing iterative sampling; and (3) an Adaptive Uncertainty Gate (AUG), which provides probabilistic forecasts by adapting uncertainty per-variable and per-horizon, corresponding to a learned decomposition of aleatoric uncertainty without manual tuning. By unifying these components, KGO achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on 13/17 ProbTS benchmarks in CRPS and 16/17 in NMAE. Further, by eliminating iterative sampling, KGO delivers at least a 25$\times$ reduction in inference time compared to iterative generative models. These results position KGO as a practical and principled framework that advances the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in probabilistic time-series forecasting, combining leading accuracy on the evaluated benchmarks with fast, single-step generation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Probabilistic time-series forecasting is essential for decision-making under uncertainty, requiring models to predict not only expected outcomes but full predictive distributions over trajectories, rather than single-point estimates [40, 43]. In applications such as energy systems, finance, and healthcare, miscalibrated uncertainty, i.e., inaccurate estimates of the range and likelihood of possible outcomes, can have severe consequences: underestimation leads to critical failures, while overestimation results in overly conservative and inefficient decisions [14, 19]. Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved the modeling of complex temporal dependencies and multimodal predictive distributions, with approaches based on flows, diffusion, and VAEs demonstrating strong empirical performance [42, 41, 50, 35, 34, 16, 30]. However, practical deployment remains challenging, as modern probabilistic forecasting systems must achieve high predictive accuracy, reliable uncertainty estimates, and efficient inference in real-world settings [43, 41]. Bridging this gap between modeling capability and deployment requirements remains central challenge in probabilistic forecasting. Correspondence to: razmar@post.bgu.ac.il. This work is not related to the authors positions at Amazon. 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Despite these advances, existing probabilistic forecasting approaches address different aspects of the problem in fragmented manner, and no single framework simultaneously captures expressive uncertainty, structured temporal dynamics, and efficient inference. First, modern generative approaches based on diffusion and flow matching provide flexible modeling of complex, multimodal predictive distributions, but rely on iterative sampling procedures whose computational cost scales with the number of steps, limiting their applicability in large-scale or real-time settings [41, 46, 28, 7]. Second, many methods compress the historical context into single representation, either as an explicit latent state, as in latent-variable and Koopman-based models, or through local conditioning mechanisms such as last-patch representations. While latent-variable approaches enable structured temporal evolution, they typically tie uncertainty to the initial state, inducing variability through its propagation rather than modeling how uncertainty evolves over time. This results in tight coupling between temporal dynamics and uncertainty modeling, limiting flexibility in how predictive distributions are formed, while local conditioning strategies can obscure long-range dependencies and limit extrapolation across extended horizons [40, 50, 30]. Finally, existing approaches often adopt fixed or heuristic strategies for uncertainty modeling, treating uncertainty in global or implicit manner, despite the fact that predictability, and thus the appropriate level of uncertainty, varies across variables and forecast horizons [25, 26]. Together, these limitations highlight the need for unified approach that jointly supports efficient generation, models temporal dynamics, and adapts uncertainty to the underlying predictability of the data. To address these limitations, we argue that probabilistic forecasting should be viewed as modeling the evolution of structured uncertainty over time, rather than predicting distributions in static manner or generating samples through iterative simulation. Future outcomes arise from underlying temporal dynamics, implying that effective forecasting requires representations that preserve and extrapolate this structure across the prediction horizon. At the same time, uncertainty is inherently heterogeneous: the predictability of future observations varies across variables and time, suggesting that uncertainty should be adapted to the underlying signal rather than treated uniformly. This perspective reframes forecasting as transformation of uncertainty governed by temporal structure, rather than static prediction or an iterative generative process. It suggests decoupling temporal evolution from uncertainty modeling, allowing each to be handled in principled and efficient manner. To instantiate this perspective, we propose KGO, unified framework for probabilistic forecasting. In contrast to prior Koopman-based approaches that evolve latent states and rely on sampling-based decoding, KGO directly models the transport from noise to future trajectories. At its core is Koopman Flow Matching (KoFM), formulation that replaces iterative generative processes with closed-form transformation in learned latent space [13, 4, 5]. Specifically, rather than simulating trajectories through multiple steps as in diffusion or flow-based models, KoFM learns structured transport that maps noise to future samples via linear evolution, enabling expressive yet tractable dynamics and efficient single-step generation. To support this mechanism, we introduce Koopman Patch Embedding (KoPE), which constructs latent representations that preserve temporal structure and admit extrapolation across the forecast horizon. By lifting observed time series into space where evolution can be modeled in structured manner, KoPE provides the state representation on which KoFM operates. Finally, to account for heterogeneous uncertainty, we propose an Adaptive Uncertainty Gate (AUG) that modulates the contribution of deterministic and stochastic components based on the predictability of each variable and horizon, allowing the model to allocate uncertainty dynamically. Together, these components realize forecasting as transformation of structured uncertainty, yielding accurate probabilistic forecasts with efficient inference. We evaluate KGO on the ProbTS benchmark [52] and observe consistent improvements across wide range of probabilistic forecasting tasks. KGO achieves the lowest CRPS on 13/17 evaluated settings and the lowest NMAE on 16/17, with strong results in both regimes: it ranks first on 7/9 long-term datasets in CRPS and 9/9 in NMAE, and on 6/8 short-term datasets in CRPS and 7/8 in NMAE. Notably, KGO enables single-step inference, yielding over 25 faster inference than iterative methods. Ablation studies show that replacing KoPE with last-patch representation, the sLSTM encoder with Transformer, or KoFM with normalizing-flow head increases average CRPS by 16.9%, 4.7%, and 9.4%, respectively. These results demonstrate that modeling forecasting as the evolution of structured uncertainty yields both strong predictive accuracy and substantial gains in inference efficiency. 2 Contributions. We introduce the Koopman Generative Operator (KGO), framework for probabilistic time-series forecasting that models prediction as the evolution of structured uncertainty rather than iterative generative sampling. 1. unifying perspective. We formulate probabilistic forecasting as the evolution of structured uncertainty, providing an alternative to iterative diffusion and flow-based generation and motivating transport-based view of prediction. 2. unified methodology. We develop KGO, which integrates (i) Koopman Patch Embedding (KoPE) for structured latent evolution, (ii) Koopman Flow Matching (KoFM) for closedform, single-step probabilistic generation, and (iii) an Adaptive Uncertainty Gate (AUG) for per-variable, per-horizon uncertainty modeling. Together, these components bridge the gap between temporal structure, expressive uncertainty, and efficient inference. 3. Strong empirical performance. On the ProbTS benchmark, KGO achieves state-of-the-art results on 29/34 configurations, improving CRPS by up to 27%, and reducing iterative inference cost by at least 25 .

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: 2.1 Deterministic Time-Series Forecasting Classical time-series forecasting has long relied on statistical models such as ARIMA [8] and vector autoregression [44], which provide strong theoretical foundations but struggle with complex non-linearities and high-dimensional dependencies. The advent of deep learning introduced more expressive models, including recurrent architectures such as LSTMs and GRUs [12, 18], which improved flexibility but remain limited in capturing long-range temporal dependencies. Recent approaches have explored wide range of architectures, including convolutional, Transformer-based, and MLP-based models [49, 36, 51, 48, 38, 37, 31]. Among these, Transformer and MLP-based methods have emerged as dominant paradigms due to their ability to model long-range dependencies and scale to high-dimensional data. More recently, there has been renewed interest in recurrent architectures through the development of xLSTM and its variants [6, 24, 23, 1], which improve memory capacity and training stability, making them competitive with modern sequence models. Despite these advances, these methods primarily produce point forecasts and do not model predictive uncertainty, limiting their applicability in decision-making settings where uncertainty is critical. 2.2 Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting Probabilistic time-series forecasting has been addressed through range of approaches that differ in how predictive distributions are modeled and generated. Early methods such as DeepAR [43] and DeepState [40] parameterize simple distributions conditioned on historical context, offering efficient inference but limited expressivity. To capture more complex, multimodal distributions, subsequent works have introduced generative models based on normalizing flows [42], variational autoencoders [50], and diffusion and flow matching-based approaches [41, 46, 22, 34, 30]. From the perspective of generation, diffusion and flow-based methods excel in predicting distributions via flexible generative transport processes, but rely on iterative sampling procedures whose computational cost scales with the number of steps, limiting their use in real-time settings [30]. This has led to the perception of trade-off between expressivity and efficiency, which we address by enabling flexible probabilistic modeling with single-step inference. In terms of temporal modeling, Koopman-based approaches impose structured, approximately linear dynamics in learned latent space for sequence prediction and forecasting [5, 29, 47, 33]. This principle has also been extended to probabilistic and generative sequence modeling [35, 50, 53], where latent uncertainty is propagated through structured dynamics. In contrast, many forecasting architectures capture temporal dependencies implicitly through learned conditioning mechanisms, without explicitly constraining the evolution of the latent state [36]. 2VAE [50] models uncertainty through latent initial state sampled from learned posterior, whose deterministic evolution induces distribution over future trajectories. In contrast, KGO decouples temporal evolution from generative modeling: Koopman dynamics structure latent trajectories, while generative operator directly maps source noise to future observations, allowing uncertainty to be modeled at the level of the forecasted sequence. Beyond modeling predictive distributions, KGO explicitly learns how to balance deterministic and stochastic predictions across variables and forecast horizons.

We propose to view probabilistic forecasting as modeling the evolution of structured uncertainty over time. Under this perspective, future trajectories arise from underlying temporal dynamics that govern both the signal and its uncertainty, rather than being generated independently or through repeated sampling procedures. This view imposes three key requirements on an effective forecasting model: (i) efficient generation, enabling direct sampling of future trajectories without iterative simulation; (ii) structured temporal evolution, allowing the model to encode and extrapolate dynamics over long horizons; and (iii) adaptive uncertainty, capturing the fact that predictability varies across variables and forecast horizons. These considerations motivate unified approach that explicitly models forecasting as the evolution of structured uncertainty, jointly satisfying the above requirements within single framework. 3.2 Overview of KGO We realize this perspective through KGO, unified framework for probabilistic forecasting that models prediction as the evolution of structured uncertainty. KGO consists of three main components: (i) Koopman Flow Matching (KoFM) module that enables efficient, single-step generation of future trajectories, (ii) Koopman Patch Embedding (KoPE) module that encodes and extrapolates temporal dynamics in structured latent space, and (iii) an Adaptive Uncertainty Gate (AUG) that dynamically balances deterministic and stochastic predictions according to the predictability of the data. Although these components are conceptually introduced in terms of their roles, their implementation follows different dependency structure. In particular, KGO first constructs latent representation of the historical context, which is then extrapolated into the future by KoPE. The resulting sequence of latent states conditions KoFM, which generates probabilistic forecasts in single step. Finally, AUG fuses the outputs of deterministic and probabilistic decoding streams to produce the final prediction. In parallel, deterministic decoder produces point forecast, ˆxdet L+1:L+H , from the same latent trajectory via residual MLP. The two outputs are combined by AUG to yield the final prediction. In the long-term forecasting regime, KGO is particularly dominant, ranking first on 7/9 datasets in CRPS and 9/9 in NMAE. By comparison, the closest competitor, 2VAE, attains only 2/9 first-place results in CRPS and none in NMAE. Notable gains are observed on ETTh2-L, where KGO reduces CRPS by more than 27% and NMAE by more than 13% relative to 2VAE. Similarly, on Weather-L, KGO reduces CRPS by approximately 26% and NMAE by approximately 18% relative to 2VAE. In the short-term forecasting regime, KGO also delivers the best overall performance, obtaining 13 of the 16 best scores 7 across CRPS and NMAE, compared with 3 for 2VAE, the next strongest baseline. The largest gains are on the ETT datasets, where KGO reduces CRPS relative to 2VAE by approximately 23% on ETTm1-S, 25% on ETTm2-S, and 19% on ETTh2-S. Overall, these findings position KGO as leading method for probabilistic time-series forecasting across the evaluated benchmarks. In particular, KGO substantially outperforms prior flow-based approaches such as Trans MAF, while also surpassing stronger generative baselines such as 2VAE. 4.3 Efficiency To assess the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency, we benchmark KGO against the same ProbTS baselines on forecast quality (CRPS, NMAE), inference latency, and peak GPU memory. All models are evaluated with matched context/horizon lengths, batch size 1, FP32 precision, and 100 forecast trajectories per window on the same hardware. KGO is channel-independent, processing variates in parallel, while future patches and generated samples are batched within the decoder. For fixed patch size and latent dimensions, inference computation and decoder activation memory scale linearly in each of these axes when all samples are processed together. sections.content: 5.1 Representation and Architecture Figure 3: Architecture ablations averaged across datasets and forecasting horizons (lower CRPS is better). Panels evaluate the four core design choices underlying KGO: latent trajectory representation (KoPE), sequence encoder, deterministicprobabilistic coupling (AUG), and generative decoder (KoFM; each head used alone, without the gate or deterministic branch). Koopman-based latent rollout, sLSTM encoding, adaptive gating, and closed-form Koopman transport yield the lowest average CRPS. Full results appear in Appendices E.1E.4. In this section, we ablate the three main components, KoPE, KoFM, and AUG, as well as the backbone choice (sLSTM), reporting CRPS averaged over datasets and forecasting horizons  (Fig. 3)  . Across 36 datasethorizon pairs, KoPE achieves lower average CRPS (0.141) than both the Last Patch baseline (0.165) and the Context Pooling head (0.165). The two non-Koopman alternatives perform nearly identically, indicating that the gain arises from the Koopman-based representation propagated to the decoder. Consistent with this, the dominant eigenvalues of the learned KoPE operator recover the daily and weekly cycles of the data (App. F.2.1). On the encoder side, holding depth and width fixed, replacing the sLSTM backbone with either Transformer or Linear RNN degrades average CRPS (0.141 vs. 0.148 and 0.145, respectively), suggesting that recurrent backbones are better suited than attention-based alternatives in this setting. Combining the deterministic and probabilistic streams through AUG gives the lowest average CRPS among the coupling variants (0.141, vs. 0.144 for conditioning KoFM on the deterministic prediction and 0.142 for fixed residual addition), although the margins are small. AUG thus matches fixed coupling rules in accuracy while adaptively modeling aleatoric uncertainty, learning the contribution of the stochastic branch per variable and forecast horizon (App. F.3). Finally, with each generative head used alone (no gate or deterministic branch) and trained with its native loss, replacing KoFM with either single-step VAE or normalizing flow head increases average CRPS by 7.2% and 9.4%, respectively, demonstrating that KoFM, the closedform Koopman push-forward, produces stronger predictive distribution than standard one-shot generative heads. 5.2 Flow Matching To investigate KoFMs ability to deliver accurate predictions while keeping inference efficient, we compare KGO against Sundial-base-128m [30], strong pretrained flow-matching foundation model, by sweeping its Euler-ODE step budget and tracing the resulting accuracyefficiency trade-off in CRPS, NMAE, and inference latency per window  (Fig. 4)  . sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented the Koopman Generative Operator (KGO), probabilistic forecasting framework that reinterprets prediction as the evolution of structured uncertainty in Koopman latent space. By combining Koopman Patch Embedding (KoPE) for consistent latent trajectory extrapolation, Koopman Flow Matching (KoFM) for closed-form, single-step generation, and an Adaptive Uncertainty Gate (AUG) for adaptive, horizonand variable-aware uncertainty modeling, KGO unifies structure, expressivity, and efficiency within single model. Empirically, this design yields state-of-the-art accuracy on 29/34 ProbTS configurations, in both shortand long-term forecasting, while reducing inference cost by over an order of magnitude compared to iterative generative methods. These results highlight the advantage of embedding generative modeling within linearizable latent dynamics, enabling both principled uncertainty propagation and scalable inference. More broadly, KGO suggests new perspective on probabilistic forecasting: rather than treating generation and dynamics as separate processes, they can be jointly governed through operator-theoretic evolution. An important direction for future work is to develop unified Koopman framework that simultaneously models evolution in physical time and transport time, further bridging dynamical systems and generative modeling.

The isolated high-magnitude modes outside the bulk include the seasonal modes discussed in App. F.2.1. 37 F.3 Uncertainty Gate Predictability in time series varies across both forecast horizons and variates: longer-range forecasts generally involve greater uncertainty, while different underlying processes and measurement conditions introduce different levels of noise. AUG accommodates this heterogeneity by learning the relative contributions of deterministic and stochastic predictions through the forecasting objective. Its weights describe the contributions of the two branches and should not be interpreted as direct estimates of aleatoric uncertainty. Figure 8 shows the stochastic weight across forecast steps (vertical axis) and variates (horizontal axis) for eight representative datasethorizon pairs. Three structures stand out. First, except on Traffic, the first forecast steps are the most deterministic and the stochastic weight rises with lead time (on Exchange-L from 0.27 to around 0.8): the immediate future is well predicted from the recent context, while aleatoric uncertainty accumulates further ahead. Second, the short-term panels keep substantial deterministic share (mean weight 0.64 on ETTm1-S), whereas on most long-term datasets the gate is nearly fully stochastic beyond the first steps. Third, the gate distinguishes variates: on ILI-L the noisy influenza-like-illness rates are almost fully stochastic (0.98), while the slowly changing number of reporting providers relies more on the deterministic branch (0.78). Together, these views show that AUG places more weight on the stochastic branch where aleatoric uncertainty is expected to be larger.
